quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what cover factor measures and the vocabulary around it.

questions.q: The relative cover of one set of threads is
questions.explain: Cover = d ÷ p, the fraction of the width occupied by yarn; p ÷ d would be greater than 1 for any real cloth.

questions.q: In K = n√tex, the maximum value of 2670 corresponds to
options: the threads of that set touching side by side
the densest fabric an airjet loom can weave
questions.explain: At K = 2670 the diameter equals the spacing, so relative cover is 1 — no gap is left between neighbouring threads of that set.

questions.q: In the Ne version of the cover factor, one set of threads reaches full cover at about
questions.explain: With d ≈ 1/(28√Ne) inch, threads touch when n ÷ √Ne = 28; 2670 is the tex-system maximum.

questions.q: Cloth cover is simply the warp cover plus the weft cover.
questions.explain: The two sets overlap where they cross, so C = C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂; 0.50 + 0.75 gives 0.875, not 1.25.

questions.q: The diameter formula d (mm) = √tex ÷ 26.7 assumes
options: a yarn specific volume of 1.1 cm³/g
questions.explain: The 26.7 comes from packing the fibre mass into a circular yarn with a specific volume of about 1.1 cm³/g (Lecture FD-12).

questions.q: The 'total cover factor' used against the airjet limits is
options: the cloth cover C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂
questions.explain: The mill adds the two Ne cover factors: 24.1 + 12.5 = 36.7. The cloth cover formula is a separate measure of covered area.

questions.q: The weave divisor is used to
options: convert tex cover factors to Ne
convert a non-plain construction into its plain-weave equivalent before checking the limits
questions.explain: Twills and satins can be set denser than plain, so dividing their K by the factor (1.22–1.73) gives the plain-equivalent that the limits refer to.

questions.q: Wider airjet looms tolerate a higher total cover factor than narrower ones.
questions.explain: The opposite: the pick must travel further, so a 134 in loom has a standard limit of 25 against 36 for a 75 in loom.

questions.q: 'Relative cover 86.2 %' for the warp in the worksheet is obtained from
questions.explain: Relative cover = K(Ne) ÷ 28 = 0.862. Dividing by 2670 mixes the tex and Ne systems; 24.15 ÷ 36.67 is the warp share of total cover, not its relative cover.

questions.q: A relative cover of exactly 1 for the weft means
options: the picks lie side by side touching
questions.explain: Cover 1 for one set means d = p for that set only; cloth cover also needs the warp, and real opacity depends on yarn flattening too.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The formulas behind cover factor and how it moves when count, density or weave change.

questions.q: The yarn diameter in millimetres from tex is
questions.explain: Diameter grows with the square root of linear density: 25 tex gives 5 ÷ 26.7 = 0.187 mm.

questions.q: If the warp count changes from Ne 20 to Ne 40 at the same 108 EPI, the warp cover factor
options: falls by a factor of √2 (about 29 % less)
questions.explain: K = EPI ÷ √Ne; √40 is √2 times √20, so K drops from 24.1 to 17.1. Halving would need a four-fold change in count.

questions.q: In the tex system, doubling the tex of the yarn at the same threads per 100 mm multiplies K by
questions.explain: K = n√tex, so K scales with the square root of tex, matching the diameter.

questions.q: The cloth cover of a fabric with warp cover C₁ and weft cover C₂ is
questions.explain: The overlap C₁C₂ is counted twice in the simple sum and must be removed once.

questions.q: A yarn of 25 tex is set at 267 threads per 100 mm. Find the tex cover factor K = n√tex.
For K = 1,335 in the tex system, what is the relative cover of that set? Give two decimals.
Which weave in the table can be set the densest before reaching the airjet limit, judged by its divisor?
questions.explain: The larger the divisor, the more raw cover the weave can carry for the same plain-equivalent; the 1/8 satin with the fewest interlacings has the highest at 1.73.

questions.q: The weave divisor for plain weave is 1.00, so its cover factor is compared with the limits unchanged.
questions.explain: The limits are defined for plain weave; all other weaves are divided by a factor above 1 to bring them to plain equivalent.

questions.q: The warp cover factor in the mill version is
questions.explain: 108 ÷ √20 = 24.15. Multiplying by √Ne would make finer yarns look denser, the opposite of reality.

questions.q: Raising the EPI from 108 to 118 at Ne 20 raises the warp cover factor by about
questions.explain: ΔK = 10 ÷ √20 = 10 ÷ 4.47 = 2.24. Ten is the change in EPI, not in K.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Reproduce the worksheet for 20×20/108×56 and a few neighbouring constructions.

questions.q: Warp Ne 20 at 108 ends per inch. Warp cover factor K = EPI ÷ √Ne, to two decimals?
Weft Ne 20 at 56 picks per inch. Weft cover factor to two decimals?
questions.explain: Cover factor in English counts = PPI ÷ √Ne = 56 ÷ √20 = 56 ÷ 4.472 = 12.52.

questions.q: Total cover factor of 20×20/108×56, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 24.15 + 12.52 = 36.67 — right at the 75 in airjet standard of 36.

questions.q: Relative cover of the warp (K ÷ 28) for a warp cover factor of 24.15, as a percentage to one decimal?
questions.explain: 24.15 ÷ 28 = 0.862, i.e. 86.2 % of the warp width is yarn.

questions.q: Warp relative cover is 0.862 and weft relative cover 0.447. Cloth cover C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂ as a percentage, to one decimal?
A 36 tex yarn is set at 334 threads per 100 mm. Tex cover factor K?
Yarn diameter in mm for a 25 tex yarn, using d = √tex ÷ 26.7. Give three decimals.
The same 20×20/108×56 construction is woven as a 2/2 twill (divisor 1.34). Plain-equivalent cover factor to two decimals?
questions.explain: 36.67 ÷ 1.34 = 27.37, well inside even the 110 in standard of 28.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Can it be woven? Weavability decisions for the airjet shed.

questions.q: 20×20/108×56 plain (total cover 36.7) is offered to a 134 in airjet loom (standard 25, upper limit 32). It is
options: weavable only at the upper limit
not weavable as plain on that loom
weavable if the warp count is coarsened
questions.explain: 36.7 is well above even the upper limit of 32 for the 134 in loom; coarsening the count would raise K further.

questions.q: If the same 20×20/108×56 is woven as a 3/1 drill (divisor 1.3), its plain-equivalent cover is 28.2, which means it
options: now fits a 110 in loom within its upper limit of 32
fits a 134 in loom within its standard of 25
questions.explain: 36.67 ÷ 1.3 = 28.2: above the 110 in standard of 28 but under its upper limit of 32, and still above 25 for the 134 in loom.

questions.q: Construction 16×12/128×60 (warp Ne 16, weft Ne 12). Total cover factor to one decimal?
questions.explain: 128 ÷ 4 = 32.0; 60 ÷ 3.464 = 17.3; total 49.3 — far beyond any plain-weave limit.

questions.q: That 49.3 construction is to be woven as a 3/1 drill (divisor 1.3) on a 75 in loom (standard 36, upper 37.5). The plain-equivalent 37.9 means it is
options: just over the upper limit — marginal at best
weavable only on a 134 in loom
weavable if the weave is changed to plain
questions.explain: 49.3 ÷ 1.3 = 37.9, slightly above 37.5. Plain weave would make it worse; wider looms have lower limits, not higher.

questions.q: A 75 in airjet loom can be pushed to a plain-equivalent total cover of about 37.5, above its standard figure of 36.
questions.explain: The table gives a standard of 36 and an upper limit of 37.5 for the 75 in loom; above that the construction is unweavable.

questions.q: A construction is 3 % over the limit. The least disruptive way to make it weavable is usually to
options: reduce the picks per inch slightly
move it to a wider loom
change the warp count to a coarser yarn
questions.explain: PPI is set at the loom and lowering it reduces weft K directly; wider looms tolerate less cover and a coarser yarn raises K.

questions.q: The warp of 20×20/108×56 has K = 24.15. What is the highest PPI in Ne 20 weft that keeps the total at the 75 in standard of 36? Round down to a whole pick.
questions.explain: Weft K may be 36 − 24.15 = 11.85; PPI = 11.85 × √20 = 53.0 picks per inch.

questions.q: Two orders for a 110 in loom (upper limit 32): a 2/2 twill with raw K = 40, and a plain with K = 32. Which is the safer to accept?
options: The plain — its K is lower
The twill — its plain-equivalent is 29.9, under the limit, while the plain sits exactly on it
questions.explain: 40 ÷ 1.34 = 29.9 leaves a margin; the plain at 32 has none. Comparing raw K across weaves is the classic mistake.

questions.q: A 1/5 satin with raw total cover 45 (divisor 1.51) can be woven on a 110 in airjet loom.
questions.explain: 45 ÷ 1.51 = 29.8, between the 110 in standard of 28 and its upper limit of 32 — weavable, though not with much margin.

questions.q: Why does the airjet limit fall as the loom gets wider?
options: The air must carry the pick across a longer shed, so a denser cloth makes insertion unreliable
questions.explain: The lecture explains that inserting the pick over a longer distance is what makes wide looms less tolerant of cover.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Mixed harder questions: unit mix-ups, limits and two-step cover calculations.

questions.q: A 40 tex yarn is set at 300 threads per 100 mm. Tex cover factor K, to the nearest whole number?
A student computes the warp relative cover as 24.15 ÷ 2670 = 0.009. The error is
options: dividing an Ne-system cover factor by the tex-system maximum
questions.explain: 24.15 is in the Ne system whose maximum is 28; 2670 belongs with K = n√tex. The correct relative cover is 24.15 ÷ 28 = 0.862.

questions.q: Warp relative cover 0.862 and weft relative cover 0.60. Cloth cover as a percentage to one decimal?
Doubling the picks of 20×20/108×56 to 112 at the same weft count makes the total cover factor about
questions.explain: Weft K doubles from 12.52 to 25.04; total = 24.15 + 25.04 = 49.2. 73.3 doubles the whole total, including the unchanged warp.

questions.q: At 108 ends per inch, what warp count Ne would make the warp threads just touch (K = 28)? Give two decimals.
questions.explain: K = EPI ÷ √Ne = 28 → √Ne = 108 ÷ 28 = 3.857 → Ne = 14.88. Any coarser count would need fewer ends to fit.

questions.q: Rank these weaves from least to most able to carry raw cover: 2/1 drill, 2/2 twill, 1/5 satin, 1/8 satin.
questions.explain: Divisors rise with fewer interlacings: 1.22, 1.34, 1.51, 1.73 in that order.

questions.q: Every weave divisor in the lecture's table is greater than 1, because no listed weave interlaces more often than plain weave.
questions.explain: Plain weave interlaces at every crossing; every rib, twill and satin interlaces less, so each gets a divisor above 1 (from 1.22 to 1.73).

questions.q: To weave 20×20/108×56 (K 36.67) on a 134 in loom within its upper limit of 32, the smallest change of weave that works is
options: it needs at least a 1/8 satin
questions.explain: 36.67 ÷ 1.22 = 30.1, already under 32. The warp rib (36.67 ÷ 1.26 = 29.1) also works but is a bigger change than the 2/1 drill.

questions.q: Using d ≈ 1 ÷ (28√Ne) inch, what is the diameter of an Ne 20 yarn in inches? Give four decimals.
questions.explain: 28 × 4.472 = 125.2; 1 ÷ 125.2 = 0.0080 in, so 125 such threads would just fill an inch.

questions.q: A construction has total cover 30 and is woven in plain weave on a 110 in loom (standard 28, upper 32). The planner's correct note is
options: above standard but under the upper limit — expect some difficulty
fine, because the weave divisor brings it to 22
questions.explain: 30 lies between 28 and 32; plain weave has divisor 1.00, so there is no correction to apply.
